title: The farewell pilgrimage
hook: the Prophet ﷺ performs his one Hajj with a vast crowd

segments.voice: Yesterday, wufud, when tribes came from every corner of Arabia and found the door open. Your line was they came from everywhere. Who did you welcome well? Day two hundred eighty-four.

A photo of the Hajj looks like water moving: a sea of people around the Ka'ba, the men in the same two plain white cloths. Those rites go back to one journey. In the tenth year after the hijra, the Prophet ﷺ announced he was going to Mecca for the pilgrimage. It was the only Hajj he made after leaving Mecca, and word spread fast. People came from all over Arabia to go with him, so many that the reports say you could look to your right and left and in front and behind and see only pilgrims. Today, the one Hajj.
screen: `A SEA OF WHITE.` → `HIS ONLY HAJJ.` → `PILGRIMS AS FAR AS THE EYE COULD SEE.`

segments.voice: Much of what we know comes from one long hadith in Sahih Muslim, told by a companion named Jabir, who walks us through the pilgrimage step by step, almost like a travel diary. At a place outside Medina, the Prophet put on ihram, the state of the pilgrim, and for the men that meant two unstitched white cloths. A king and a shepherd look exactly the same in them. Then he began to call out the talbiyah, and the crowd called it with him. It starts: labbayk, Allahumma, labbayk. Here I am, O God, here I am. Labbayk is the answer you give when someone calls your name and you come running. Jabir describes him circling the Ka'ba, walking between the hills of Safa and Marwah, standing at Arafah, throwing stones at Mina. And along the way, the Prophet said something that explains why Muslims still perform Hajj in almost exactly these steps: take your rites from me, for I may not make the pilgrimage again after this year. He was teaching by doing, and he seems to have known it was the last chance. That's why it's called the farewell pilgrimage. Today, the men still wear the same two white cloths. Women wear modest clothing, which may be white as well. And the call is the same one Jabir heard: here I am. All in white, all saying the same thing, all equal.
screen: `JABIR'S LONG HADITH.` · `IHRAM — KING AND SHEPHERD ALIKE.` · `LABBAYK — HERE I AM.` · `TAKE YOUR RITES FROM ME.` · then, large: `ALL IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a crowd all in white. Sit, and close your eyes if you like. See the plain, a huge crowd, and every person dressed the same. You can't tell who's rich, who's famous, who's in charge. Now put yourself in it, in the same plain cloth, with nothing that marks you out. Notice what that feels like: lighter, maybe, or strange. If you pray, you can whisper the pilgrim's words: here I am. If you don't, just rest in the crowd. The bell holds the time.
Labbayk. The answer pilgrims called back to God during the Prophet's one Hajj, made with a vast crowd, not long before he died. Today's word.
Your line: all in white. Today, when you size someone up by their clothes, their car or their title, picture them in plain white cloth and look again. Day two hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims able to afford it and physically able are required to make the Hajj once in their lives; pilgrims enter ihram, men in two white unstitched cloths, and follow the rites the Prophet performed on his farewell pilgrimage, calling the talbiyah as they go.

fork.setup: you're leading a vast crowd of pilgrims, and you may not come back. how do you teach the rites?
options: write them down and send the list to every tribe.
do them in front of everyone and say: take your rites from me.
leave it to each tribe's custom.
fork.reveal: he taught by doing: take your rites from me, for I may not make the pilgrimage again after this year. Muslims still follow those steps.

original.note: Arabic: here I am, at your service. the first word of the talbiyah, called by pilgrims.

trapdoor: what you thought: a big religious trip.
what it means: his one Hajj, taught by doing, with everyone dressed the same and answering the same call.
what a scholar hears: Jabir's hadith in Sahih Muslim is the main source for the Prophet's Hajj, and take your rites from me makes his actions the model for the rites.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1218 (Jabir's account of the Prophet's Hajj)
Sahih Muslim 1297 (take your rites from me; I may not perform Hajj after this year)

notes: Hadith numbers (Muslim 1218, 1297; Bukhari 1549) cited from memory; confirm.
'As far as the eye could see' paraphrases Jabir's description of the crowd in Muslim 1218; confirm.
Modern Hajj size given as 'about two million people or more in a normal year'; numbers vary widely by year. Confirm or soften.
Women's ihram described as modest clothing, often white; confirm with the Keeper that this is stated appropriately across schools.
Place of entering ihram (Dhul-Hulayfah) left unnamed.
